To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

thiamine deficiency and ethanol interact to cause focal degeneration of the thalamus and that this is associated with neuroimmune gene induction and microglial activation and that the thalamic degeneration is associated with loss of monocarboxy lic acid transporters that are necessary for the metabolism of acetate to acetyl-CoA.

ethanol potentiates thiamine deficiency-induced thalamus degeneration by inducing neuroimmune gene expression and by decreasing monocarboxylate transporter (MCT) and Acetyl-CoA synthase (AcCoA) expression in thalamus.
thiamine deficiency alone causes neurodegeneration in thalamus and entorhainic cortex but ethanol potentiates thiamine induced neurodegeneration in the thalamus, but not in the entorhainc cortex.

the neuroimmune and neurochemical mechanisms that cause focal thalamic degeneration in alcoholism.
understanding the mechanisms of Wernickee's encephalopathys-Korsakoff's syndrome, a common disorder in alcoholics, which is caused by thiamin deficiency (vitamin B1).
the mechanisms that cause Wernicke’s encephalopathy and Korsakoff’s syndrome (WE-Ks), a common neurological disease of alcoholism that is caused by thiamin (vitamin B1) deficiency (TD).

TD and EtOH interact to induce THAL neuroimmune gene activation and neurodegeneration.

TD is not a benign condition and that EtOH can potentiate TD effects.
